speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: What kind of future schools will support the future economy and the SG100 nation we want to build?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: The paper cited that most existing education systems provide highly silo-ed training, featured by a number of 20th century mindsets and practices that hinder the progress of today's talent and workforces.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Two such legacy issues burden formal education systems worldwide.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One, the traditional dichotomy between Humanities and Sciences and also the dichotomy between applied and pure training; and two, the prestige premium traditionally attached to tertiary-certified forms of education versus, say, skills mastery of other forms.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is the urgent need also to incentivise lifelong learning.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Because of the declining population of the young in countries, simply equipping the young better in schools is not enough.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Single-skillset jobs are also on the decline, they say.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This means that many jobs that require only mathematical, including computational, skills would be automated.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Similarly, jobs that require only predominantly generic social skills would not be paid well since the supply of this pool is usually large.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Schools for the future must thus try to develop students who can successfully combine mathematical and critical soft skills.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: That is the essence of good future education.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: This is confirmed by workforce consultants, such as Manpower Inc and the Centre for Creative Leadership.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: When new skills are identified as fast as other skills become extinct, the ticket to stay relevant is one's learn-ability and, that is, the willingness, capacity and capability to learn.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How do schools for the future promote and model learn-ability?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: One way, as some experts pointed out, is for the student of the future to be constantly exposed to and try new experiences, including unfamiliar subjects in school.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: But technical competencies are not the only deliverables of education, now or in the future.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: More so, the future education system needs to deliver students who are not frustrated or surprised by changes; students who in the face of change and failures, pick themselves up quickly and prepare themselves yet again; students who in the midst of changes retain an anchor and heed a compass that will help them retain their humanity, their loyalty and goodness.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We need students with character who will do good even when no one is watching; clean up after themselves and be comfortable in interacting on a daily basis with persons who are of different races, religions and abilities.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I recently came across the concept of the "East-West Private School" that Mr Jack Ma, billionaire-founder of Alibaba, is intending to build.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: In the Chinese website describing this school called Yun-Gu, named after Mr Jack Ma himself, Ma Yun, I learnt of the several features advertised to attract top-notch families, local and foreign, to sign up their children.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: With the mission to raise every child to be the best version of himself, Mr Jack Ma said that the unique features are as follows: that it will be a 15-year school syllabi covering from preschool up to high school.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There will be an open, sharing, green smart-campus with a strong foundation in technology, using big data, cloud computing and the works.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There will be a curriculum based on bilingualism, porosity amongst schools, society and nature, strong Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) focus, physical wellness and life skills and an appreciation for the arts.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: And there will be individualised education plans and schedules developed with students and by students as well, based on their learning ability and their areas of passion.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: I was initially excited when I read about this school that Mr Jack Ma intends to build until I analysed it more carefully.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: You see, the school that Mr Jack Ma intends to build is meant for 3,000 young people; a staff-student ratio of one is to five; with a strict entrance assessment.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: It is not a school built for a nation.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We are not a company and it is formed for the purpose of meeting the needs of every citizen, not only those who can afford private education.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Hence, I am convinced that if Singapore put our heart to it, we will be able to build even stronger schools for the future than Mr Jack Ma.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: There is much to reflect and rethink about Schools for the Future for Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: Who would we be educating in the schools for the future?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: How would content be delivered and by whom?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng (Jalan Besar)
text: We cannot tweak it a little here and there.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We have initiatives, such as Civics and Moral Education, Character and Citizenship Education, and now, Values in Action, in our school curricula.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: While we cannot deny that values and moral education are usually caught rather than taught, we cannot overlook the need to instil, nurture and exemplify good values at every opportunity we have, beginning with our schools and educators.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, when children are told to be kind, they need to understand what being kind means.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, children need to see kindness in action − role-modelled by the teacher or the parents, so that the understanding of kindness is entrenched.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In order to internalise it, children need to demonstrate kindness to others around them, be it their friends, family members, towards animals and to perfect strangers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Children learn this by observing significant adults in their lives, be it teachers, parents or adult caregivers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Hence, for our children to learn and develop values and good character, they need to have good role models and be actively involved in demonstrating those values which will shape their character.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: One way of doing this is for our children to be actively involved in community work where they help others, or in outdoor learning where they learn to engender trust and to care for the environment and for others or participating in team games where they learn about teamwork, cooperating with others and looking beyond self.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, the reality is that many students and even parents still see Civics and Moral Education, Character and Citizenship Education and now, Values in Action and NurtureSG as just another subject or programme to sit through, complete and get a passing grade in.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can such important programmes be enhanced and intertwined with one another so that the nurturing of values and development of good character are part of a more holistic education for our children in schools?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How can parents play a greater role in creating this holistic educational environment for our children?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Mr Chairman, the journey to becoming a sporting nation and achieving sporting glory at the highest level surely must start somewhere.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Look at the vibrancy of the sporting scene in the schools in the US.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: They used to send their college teams to compete at the Olympics.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Every young athlete there harbours a dream to compete for sporting glory at the highest level, be it local, national or international.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: However, the dream of becoming the next world champion, especially for a young athlete living in a small country like Singapore, should not rest on the individual and his family alone.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The nation must share that dream and it must filter down to the schools to begin with.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I remember back in the 1970s, competitions among the schools were keen and sporting rivalries were strong, all in good spirit and character building.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: There was always a lesson to be learnt, in victory or defeat.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: The New Nation, the predecessor of The New Paper, gave generous coverage to school sports with large photo spreads.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: And what you do not see often, you do not think much of it over time as well.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: How can we dream about competing against the great footballing nations at the World Cup Finals when our youths are not even fired up to compete against one another in schools?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: Sports in schools can build camaraderie, character and a sense of belonging in our youths.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat (Hougang)
text: I urge the Ministry to look into promoting a vibrant sporting culture in schools because the future of our dream for sporting glory is at stake.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Last month, in this House, we heard about the progress of the YES!

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My colleague, the hon Leon Perera, also suggested at the same Sitting that we should consider a "push" model instead of the current approach.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Schools and other programmes are open on an opt-in basis.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Through such programmes, we should let students try their hand at starting a business even when they are still in school.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Give them practical experience in thinking out of the box, selling, raising capital, even getting rejected and learning to be resilient.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Ultimately, we need to develop a mindset change in our young students in looking at life and business and how we view risks and possibilities in life.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And I believe early exposure to entrepreneurship training and development can help to bring about such a mindset change.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope we can change the mindset of our young people to consider entrepreneurship as a worthwhile ambition alongside, if not ahead of, working for the Public Service or for a multinational corporation (MNC).

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Mr Chairman, streaming has served its purpose in our education system for many years.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Most of us have lived through and probably even benefited from academic streaming during our own educational journey.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: However, with an education landscape that supports different educational pathways, greater diversity in the pursuit of excellence and in fulfilling varied aspirations, many would question the continued purpose and need for academic streaming.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: As an educator, I recognise the purpose of academic streaming.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: It helps teachers in being more focused in their teaching so that they are able to pitch their teaching content and pedagogy that are suitable for the students they teach.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: This, in turn, helps students to optimise their learning and realise their full potential.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: However, this can be done just as well through subject-based banding, without exposing students to the self-limiting structure of academic streaming.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: For students, they ought to be given a wide enough berth to discover their abilities and potential in different subjects and not feel limited by the academic stream they are in.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: For parents, academic streaming fuels their worry for their children taking the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE), to the extent that the tuition industry and proliferation of assessment books and enrichment courses for personal development have boomed because of the belief by parents that, with these interventions, the academic stream their children are eligible for and, hence, their children's future, can be assured.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: For prospective employers and the general public, their perception of individuals and their potential for success in life is largely shaped by the academic stream they were in.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Is now not the time to do away with streaming and instead provide only subject-based banding which has already been implemented in different grade levels across our schools, and which has allowed our students to realise their potential in different subjects at their own pace?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Are we still not ready to cull this sacred cow?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, we have debated the issue of class size in this House before.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Class size is distinct from teacher-student ratio, which can be affected by many other factors.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While there are different perspectives in the academic literature on the merits of smaller class sizes, some facts do stand out.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Class sizes of international schools in Singapore are smaller than in local schools.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our class sizes are still significantly higher than the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) average.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And our typical class size has not changed very much since I was a child, and I need not remind Members that was a very long time ago.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our large class sizes are supplemented by remedial classes which can provide weaker students with more focused teaching and engagement.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Students who are required to attend remedial classes may feel stigmatised and become demoralised.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Morale and self-esteem can have an effect on academic performance.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, remedial classes extend hours for students and crimp time for other kinds of academic or character development.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This could be a double hurdle, maybe even a regressive effect, for children with limited language skills, especially those from disadvantaged backgrounds.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Does MOE have any plans to study this further and review this in the curriculum?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: At the rate they are glorified, celebrity tutors are on their way of reaching stardom, much like their counterparts in Hong Kong where their faces are splashed all over the train station billboards.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: However, often, it is the elephant in the room that is being ignored, at least by MOE in public.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: There is a rightful place for additional education help outside school hours.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: This is especially so for students who are academically weaker and at risk of not being able to catch up.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Besides having the tuition industry diminish the good work that MOE has put in, the habit of tuition, regardless of one's real needs, will produce students whose learning habits and styles may run counter to what is required in the future economy, the future economy being one which highly favours self-driven learners with a high learnability quotient, meaning a high degree of willingness and capability of learning new skills quickly.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: To this end, I urge the Ministry to adopt the following strategies to counter the further advancement of a "tuition-nation".

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Two, further support the not-for-profit organisations, such as self-help groups, the Community Development Councils (CDCs) and anchor preschool operators more strategically.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Strengthen their ability to help those who need help.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: This can come in the form of training tutors, deploying MOE teachers to work in these outfits and investing in additional resources for their charges.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Three, engage families who are willing and able to support their own children, for instance, in regular MOE-organised bootcamps to update them on syllabi, learning outcomes and assessment methodologies.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: And lastly, in the longer term, gradually lower the stakes by seriously introducing other forms of assessments so that the focus on academic rat-racing is reduced.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Mr Chairman, this is the second year in a row that I am raising the issue of equitable funding for schools.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: The Minister's replies, when I brought up the issue twice last year, were along the lines that MOE resources schools based on the needs of students, programmes offered by the schools and the enrolment of the schools.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: In other words, MOE does acknowledge that there exists a distinct disparity in funding between the brand name schools and the other schools.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: I have highlighted that the per capita funding for schools favours popular schools with high enrolment.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Parents can see the disparity for themselves, which manifests in differences in the range of arts, sports and enrichment programmes offered by schools.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: When this information makes its way through the grapevine, the perception that certain schools offer more and better opportunities for student development will perpetuate.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: This drives the enrolment numbers for the schools and, consequently, the amount of funding that the Government disburses to them, based on enrolment figures.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Even without factoring in the higher fees, greater economies of scale and contributions by well-connected alumni, the brand name schools are already competing in a league of their own.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: If per capita funding is the great leveller in developing our students fully and holistically in all schools, why did MOE need to close down seven neighbourhood schools last year?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Falling enrolment numbers should not be a reason for these schools to shut their doors then because the Government is still committed to funding them on a per capita basis.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: When some schools are forced to do more or the same with less, while others are spoilt for choice in terms of what they can offer their students, can we say that this model of funding is in the best interest of every student?

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: Last year, my colleague, Mr Dennis Tan, asked the Minister if the Government takes the higher school fees and contributions from wealthy alumni into account when providing funding to schools.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: The Minister did not provide a response to that.

speaker: Mr Png Eng Huat
text: I hope the Minister can provide an answer to this important question and release details on the funding given to each school to support the notion that every school is a good school.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: MOE said, "The current T-score system grades students very finely.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It is unnecessary at this young age to make such fine distinctions between children.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The contradictory message which MOE is telling the students and the parents is that "every point counts".

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: If you do not make the PSLE score, you do not make the cut-off point, there is no discussion.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I appeal to MOE to reconsider this policy.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: You may say every school is a good school.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But students do have their aspirations, their dream choices.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For various personal reasons, they may not have opted for Direct School Admission (DSA) to be admitted to their choice secondary school.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Or they could not make it for their dream school based on DSA.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: But sometimes, their dreams, the aspirations are just within a finger's grasp away.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Because of a bad day due to illness or nervousness, they did not perform to their expectation.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: In the past, principals of schools do have some discretion to admit students on a case-by-case basis.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: They can look for students who had performed well throughout the six years of school but fumbled on PSLE day.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: It may be that the student has other skills or talents which the school may be able to develop.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: For example, a school with a tradition for swimming may be a better choice for a budding swimmer.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Our school principals are very capable civil servants.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Allow them some discretion to admit students based on their assessment or interviews.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Please do not send a wrong signal to the students that the PSLE score is everything.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Next, I wish to ask MOE about its policy on schools which deliberately set exams to such high standards so that a majority of students do not do well.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I understand that some schools pride themselves on their ability to fail a large percentage of their students during the school exams in the belief that these students will strive to do better during national exams.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: By doing so, would not the school be imposing a disproportionate level of stress on the students?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Has MOE ever studied the effect of such stress on the students?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Surely, there may be some students who are greatly discouraged by their poor results.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Some students may suffer a breakdown when they find out that they had failed a few papers despite working very hard through the year.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Why do such schools take away the joy of learning by imposing an unrealistic standard for the students?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: Could our students learn in a better and more enjoyable manner instead of expecting them to memorise everything and regurgitate them during the national exams?

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: The schools should ensure that the students are tested based on what is expected of them.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Of the 2,800 students that were successful in DSA, how many of them ended up in IP schools?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Minister Heng Swee Keat used to profess that every school is a good school.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: A good school does not necessarily mean a school that offers IP.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Rather, it is the best choice based on how closely it can meet and nurture the students' talents, academically and otherwise.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, I would like to know how MOE can help non-IP schools focus on their niche and how it can attract students to apply to non-IP schools through DSA.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: They move on to IP schools which offer School-Based Gifted Education Programmes (SBEP).

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is like a "backdoor" for the gifted students.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: A Straits Times article dated 23 January 2017 also alluded to this anomaly, when several parents interviewed said that in the most competitive schools, at least half of those admitted via DSA were academically talented, including those from GEP.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In particular, I would like to ask the Minister to consider closing the "backdoor" so schools will no longer use academic criteria to "pre-select" students under the DSA Academic scheme.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Edwin Tong, you can take both the cuts.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: MOE has previously announced that it is relooking the DSA criteria.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: This, indeed, is timely because there are several areas which, in my view, need an urgent review.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: First, I really cannot understand the meaning of DSA Academic.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: According to the MOE website, the purpose of DSA is to give students, and I quote, "an opportunity to demonstrate a more diverse range of achievements and talents in seeking admission to secondary schools".

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Why then is there a need to have this parallel admission system based on academic merit?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The parallel system can also be open to abuse, such as offering students DSA Academic on waitlist.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Why is there a need for a waitlist?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: And if a waitlist's student is confirmed only after the PSLE results are released, does that not mean that one can game the system?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: In such a case, it would then become very important to understand what the criteria for the waitlist are, but that is never published.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Like anything in life, our CCA system cannot be rigid and unbending.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: If a student gets a DSA place based on, say, athletics, first, and subsequently discovers his talent in something else, can that student be allowed to pursue that something else at the expense of athletics?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: A DSA place is for four to six years.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: We have to remember that a child at 11 or 12 will be very different from one who is 16 or 17, and our system must be flexible enough to take that into account.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Another unintended consequence of a very robust DSA system is that it leaves very little room for a student to try out new sport or experience a new art form in school.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: One has to be already very good at the CCA to even join it.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It is either you are very good at it, get a DSA place or do not join the CCA.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: So, can the Minister please look into this when reviewing the system?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I heard my colleagues take this point up earlier so I will be very short.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: The short answer the Ministry previously gave was that it is better to have a simpler system.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I can understand the merits of having a simpler system as it is easier to administer.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But we are dealing with the educational pathways of our students and a simpler system runs counter to the belief that each child is special and different.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It also cuts across the MOE's own policy of making education much more than just about numbers and grades and to look at the holistic worth of each and every individual.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: It sends the message that whatever may be the efforts to value holistic education, at the end of the day, only academic merit matters.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: I would also like to join my colleagues in urging the Minister to consider returning the discretion to consider these admissions back to the principals and the teachers.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Perhaps, give them the discretion with some parameters and guidelines so that it is not abused.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: But trust our educators with that discretion because they will consider the merits of each appeal individually.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: We have come to accept that every school is a good school.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai (Marine Parade)
text: Perhaps, we should also recognise that every child is a good child, albeit in different ways and at different paces, and that having a simpler system is not necessarily doing justice to recognising the individual intrinsic worth of each child.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Many parents are anxious to know if the current advantage given to affiliated pupils would be reduced.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Some had questioned whether giving affiliated pupils a 30- to 40-point advantage under the current system was too much.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I suggest MOE gradually do away with the current affiliation priority scheme so that all students can be more accurately placed in schools that best suit them according to their abilities.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Perhaps, the Minister can give an update on the review?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Mr Chairman, school affiliation remains a bugbear for many parents and students.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Parents whose children are not in primary schools affiliated to popular schools are worried that their children will have little chance of gaining admission to these popular schools.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Parents whose children are still in preschools are also getting very worried because they want to ensure their children can enrol in a primary school affiliated to a popular school.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: Their worries go back to preschool admission and the planning goes on for more than 10 years ahead.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar
text: How can the Ministry review the school admission process based on affiliation to make it fairer and equally accessible for students who do not come from affiliated schools to gain admission into popular schools that have affiliated feeder schools?

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: My inputs here are on how to take it to the next level.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: It is a known fact that this current support model is insufficient to effectively help those students to access the academic curriculum, not to mention the other life skills that they require in life.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The small number and the bandwidth of Allied Educators in each school mean that they can do very little to educate these students.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: In schools where there are students with different types of learning disabilities, the stress on these professionals is even worse.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: So, we need more innovative and scalable models in this space.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Next, in the Institutions of Higher Learning (IHLs), such as the ITEs, polytechnics and universities, thanks to MOE, most IHLs have now set up one-stop education support services for students and undergraduates with special needs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: However, the type and quality of support are largely inconsistent.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: We need to strengthen the handshakes between IHL students and their employers, likely in the form of a Train-Place-Train model.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: For Special Ed (SPED) schools, the SPED schools of today are in a far better state, thanks to MOE.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: One, beyond the curriculum framework drawn up by MOE's SPED department, there is a need to populate the framework with common resources.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Subjects, such as daily living skills, a domain of learning required for all students, are left to the individual voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) to develop.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Two, inclusion opportunities for many special schools remain low.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Many SPED students interact with their peers from mainstream schools only during Community Involvement Programme (CIP) and corporate social responsibility (CSR) initiatives, and not on a daily basis.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Three, talent identification, talent invitation and development in SPED schools remain challenging for the schools.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: There is not even a degree in special education offered by the Government-funded IHLs of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The SPED sector continues to compete unsuccessfully for health professionals, such as occupational therapists and speech therapists.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: But, Sir, my biggest concern lies in the dearth of learning opportunities for adults with special needs in our country.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The continued education and training for persons with special needs is an area of high priority.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Without continued training both in life and job skills, more and more will remain at home or will require external day-care help, all of which are costly options to the families and to the state.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Singapore's local workforce is forecasted to experience zero growth if our population trends remain.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: The special-needs workforce can be an important strategic asset to take on either blue-collar or white-collar jobs.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Today, the number of courses customised for the special needs workforce is miserable.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: There must be innovative ways by which the thousands of courses in the mainstream can be systematically customised to train others who learn differently.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: A SPED Academy should look into specific learning needs, solutions and across the entire lifespan of persons with special needs in our country, underpinned by the important principles of digitalisation, innovation, scalability and partnership set out by the Committee for Future Economy and analysing how the future economy and ITMs can include persons who learn and contribute differently.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: A bus academy, a rail academy, had already been set up.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: Hence, I hope my call for a SPED Academy will not be ignored.

speaker: Ms Denise Phua Lay Peng
text: If done well, I am confident the SPED Academy will be the first of its kind worldwide and can play an important role in the future education landscape and economy of Singapore.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong, you have two cuts.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: I declare my interest as President of the Society for the Physically Disabled (SPD) and Board Member of SG Enable.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, I requested that the Ministry consider specifically approaching training providers for more efficiency and greater efficacy in outcomes.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Can I know if the Ministry has paid consideration to the same?

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: As more mainstream schools embrace students with disabilities and certain special needs, I request that the Ministry consider a panel of prequalified educators, allied as well as teachers, so that such students can be appropriately cared for and effectively nurtured.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: The equipping of educators is too important to be left to individual schools to select training providers, as is the case now.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Schools, despite their expertise, may not be best equipped to choose appropriate training providers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: On the other hand, the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA) has developed a structured training programme in which preschool teachers trained in assisting children with special needs and disabilities and, together with VWOs, Government agencies, like the Workforce Development Agency (WDA) and ECDA, have developed accredited training programmes for preschool teachers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: These teachers who require training and then register to attend courses will be appointed training providers.

speaker: Ms Chia Yong Yong (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps, MOE could consider taking some reference from ECDA's model?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Mr Chairman, for many special needs students, navigating the public transport system on their own may be a daunting task.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: As a result, SPED schools and parents of special needs students depend on school buses.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: As a parent of two primary school children myself, I trudge down to the void deck of my flat to see my two kids off on their school buses on most mornings.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Our school buses are a Singaporean institution and special needs students should not be excluded from that.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: This is because the bus operators for such routes may need to deploy additional manpower for special processes and equipment that may degrade commercial viability.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: What would the VWO do if no operator wants to take up a school bus tender?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Not all VWOs have the means to buy and operate their vehicles.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Will MOE consider fresh ideas to help special needs schools address this issue?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: One suggestion is to require bus operators to support a certain number of special needs school bus routes as part of the contracting requirements under the Bus Contracting Framework.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Another idea is to apply a state subsidy to bus contracts for special needs schools to make them commercially attractive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: A one-off financial assistance package could also be applied to help school bus operators retrofit their buses to better cater to transporting special needs children, similar to the Land Transport Authority's (LTA's) assistance package rolled out in 2008 to help retrofit seat belts and provide booster seats on small buses.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Currently, dyslexia assessment is done voluntarily based on pre-assessments by preschool and primary school teachers who would then make recommendations to parents.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe it is timely for MOE to introduce mandatory and subsidised dyslexia screening at the preschool level.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An assessment performed when the child is in the second half of the second year of kindergarten would give the parents more time to prepare the child for formal schooling.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Studies have shown that early intervention helps the child to better catch up in reading and writing with their peers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Despite initiatives like the Open Door Programme, the employment rate of persons with disabilities and special needs remains low.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: If we want to build an inclusive society, we are going to have to work on changing mindsets.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Besides the benefit of having an inclusive employment policy which helps to encourage and boost further employment for PWDs, it will also expose our school children to an environment where they may grow up seeing such persons working alongside other staff.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: Together with suitable education programmes, MOE and schools can use such opportunities to help all students understand the needs of PWDs and to learn how to interact and get along respectfully and meaningfully.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong
text: We have a long way to go in equalising employment opportunities, but if we allow our students to develop respect and empathy from a young age, they are more likely to carry these attitudes with them when they enter the workforce in future or become employers.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, how many more MOE kindergartens will be set up in the next two years and whether there are plans to open them in all primary schools in Sengkang, Punggol and Hougang?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: MOE seeks to level the playing field for all children through subsidies and additional financial assistance for needy students.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Minister also share if the teachers are trained to detect students with learning difficulties and assist them?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We have appealed to the Government to put more resources to enhance early childhood education as it is an important social leveller.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I have also proposed to the Government to build larger early childhood education centres similar to our primary schools instead of tucking them in void decks and to co-locate them with the primary schools as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I am glad that the Government has responded by opening five larger capacity preschool childcare centres in each district and opened a kindergarten that is co-located within a primary school, that is, North Oaks Primary School in my division.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Larger preschools will have economies of scale and also create better career prospects for our early childhood educators.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: What are the plans in place to expand the MOE network of early childhood education centres?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We should continue to invest in the training of early childhood educators and the pedagogy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: How can we attract and encourage more talents into this very important sector?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I suggest MOE take the lead to ensure that our preschool educators are remunerated attractively and have a programme in place to retain the top talented educators in the public sector, instead of them being poached by the private tuition sector.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: We are dealing with the foundation years which are very important for our students and for our future.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: This would make it easier for Singaporean families to go overseas and regionalise and easier to integrate the children back into our school system upon their return.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng
text: And given our education branding, perhaps non-Singaporeans could even be charged premiums high enough to help cross-subsidise our own overseas Singaporeans students.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Miss Cheng, you can take both your cuts.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Chairman, the Committee on the Future Economy (CFE) suggested that in our next phase of internationalisation, Singaporeans need to spend more time in regional markets to understand them at a deeper level.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It urged the Government to "ease the concerns of Singaporean parents over their children's education while taking on overseas assignments".

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Hence, I would like to ask MOE to consider setting up more Singapore International Schools (SIS) overseas, especially in cities where there are significant Singaporean communities.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It has an excellent reputation and attracts non-Singaporean parents as well, who are drawn to our academic formula, and these schools also provide chances for our teachers to gain overseas exposure.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: The education system in Singapore has been focusing on academic grades, sports and the arts.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Due to affluence, we understand that dietary habits have become a problem for young children.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: Will the Ministry share with the House the progress of NurtureSG in inculcating healthy behaviours in our young?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What kind of skills are they taught and how is the Ministry working with parents, caregivers, schools and community institutions to create a conducive environment for them to embrace healthy dietary habits and lifestyles?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Teachers I have spoken to report the number of cases where students do not attend school for a long period of time without valid reasons.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There have been cases of parents or guardians brought to Court for neglecting to send their children to school, but it is understood that incarcerating the parent or guardian may put the child in further jeopardy.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How then would the Ministry ensure that the Compulsory Education Act will be an effective deterrent for neglectful parents?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: One recent study by the Duke-NUS Graduate Medical School linked sleep deficiency with lowered cognitive performances, deterioration of sustained attention, working memory and alertness.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Longer-term issues include high blood pressure, obesity, behavioural problems and impaired growth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: One of the recommendations from the study was to start school later.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong
text: Additionally, most schools today function as full-day schools, making it feasible to implement a later start time.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: When these 15,000 children transit from full day preschool to Primary 1 this year, many would require after school care service as well.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I also note that MOE will continue to expand the places in each school-based SCC and expand the number of schools with SCCs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Many families with both working parents, put their children in full day kindergarten.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: When the child enrols in a primary school, after-school care services are essential for this group.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: There seems to be a huge mismatch between childcare and after-school care services.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Can the Government do more to make sure that we have an accurate projection of the demand for after-school care services in each estate by the number of children in full-day kindergarten?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: Most parents prefer to put their children in SCCs that are in the same primary school as the children.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak
text: I hope MOE can ramp up the capacity and the number of SCCs to match MSF's rate of ramping up childcare centres.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: For our youths to effectively tap on these opportunities, language and cultural understanding is key.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Indeed, even basic proficiency in a language opens a window to the culture and mindset of another people.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Will MOE consider offering ASEAN languages as a third language option for more students?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: And would MOE consider working with tertiary institutions, especially their business faculties, to strongly encourage students to learn ASEAN languages, cultures and business cultures?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Could we complement these efforts and facilitate these outcomes with an increased focus on regional language proficiency in our school curricula?

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: There are other good reasons, in many ways more important reasons, for doing so.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Research has found several benefits of multilingual education in children, including cognitive and intellectual skills.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) has consistently championed multilingual education in schools.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: Second, to protect and preserve our own multiculturalism.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: We should promote the learning of our own national language and our other official languages.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: It promotes national integration, and it is our good fortune that our national language and other official languages happen to be among the most widely spoken in Asia and the world.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: We currently have third language programmes at the secondary school level like the Malay Special Programme (MSP) for learning Malay, and Chinese Special Programme (CSP) for Chinese; and we have conversational third language programmes for Malay and Chinese at the primary school level as enrichment, but not as part of the regular curriculum.

speaker: Mr Chen Show Mao (Aljunied)
text: As learning languages is best done when young, could the Ministry look into making the conversational third language programme part of the syllabus to deepen the conversational language skills of our primary school students, and we do this starting with our national language and our official languages perhaps included as part of the regular curriculum for every student, that is, compulsory and during school hours, but without the pressure of examinations?

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: The two are intertwined and cannot be separated.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Hence, a good command of Mother Tongue can help students understand their own culture and roots and stimulate their interest and passion to explore and study further.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: This will also help students to be sensitive towards other countries' culture, strengthening their world view and understanding of their own culture.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Cultivating interest in mother tongues and improving the standard cannot rely on textbooks alone.

speaker: Ms Tin Pei Ling (MacPherson)
text: Mother tongues should be used more often and in a lively manner.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Parents, grandparents, family members, teachers, neighbours and communities all owe a child varying degrees of duty to protect and nurture him and to guide him in his journey towards adulthood.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Over the years, MOE has been making the effort to strengthen the partnership between parents and schools and communities so that our children will have a better education experience.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: This is a challenging initiative as our curriculum is quite demanding and we have more families where both parents are working.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh
text: Can the Ministry provide an update on its efforts to foster stronger parental and community partnership with our schools to enrich our children's educational experiences?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A positive school-home relationship will improve communication between the school and parents, which can lead to more productive and constructive outcomes for students and for other schools as well.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Some would like a bigger involvement in their children's development and care in school.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: They feel that they have the capacity to volunteer in various areas, to contribute to the overall school experience for their children.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Other parents are less able to volunteer in schools because of work and family commitments, but still want to be involved in their child's education journey.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: A strong integrated network will enable schools and parents to better understand what is in the best interest of the children so that they can work together to develop the children's passions and strengths, both in school and at home.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Education is a key strength of our society and economy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our school system produces good educational outcomes and is internationally respected.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is inclusive and ensures that all young Singaporeans, regardless of background, have access to good educational opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our students have done very well in international studies, such as Trends in International Mathematics and Science Study (TIMSS) and the Programme for International Student Assessment (PISA), which emphasise application, reasoning and problem-solving skills.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We take a long view of education, constantly reviewing what and how we teach to cater to the aspirations and needs of our students and the needs of our economy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For example, we are focusing more on 21st Century competencies, such as critical and inventive thinking, and soft skills, such as communication skills and cultural awareness.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: At the core of our education are values and character.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They anchor and guide our students in navigating the uncertainties and challenges of the future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I am glad this has been well-received by parents and educators alike.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We owe a big part of our success to our professional and dedicated educators.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Every time I meet them, I see them always strive to bring out the best in every child and never failing to impress me with their ideas and hard work.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our mission in the Ministry of Education (MOE) is to mould the future of the nation by moulding the people who will determine the future of the nation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is not just MOE's work but the collective work of educators, parents and the wider community.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Together, we want to build in our children a strong foundation of knowledge, skills and values that will enable them to chase their dreams.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Debates on how we are changing our education system, like this one here today, will become more important, as the world is changing at an unprecedented rate.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Ms Denise Phua asked how we will help schools, educators and students respond to a volatile, uncertain, complex and ambiguous (VUCA) world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In my conversations with employers, parents and educators, many are likewise concerned and want to know how the education system will better prepare our young for the future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: What do all these structural shifts mean for our young and for education?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In the area of knowledge and skills, our young need to develop deep skills and to continue to update these skills and acquire new ones to stay relevant.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In terms of qualities and attitudes, they have to be more adaptable to reskill themselves as needed.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They have to be more resilient to navigate changes and uncertainties ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They also have to be more enterprising so that they can innovate and create value.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: By making a big push towards lifelong learning, we have already started to lay the groundwork for the changes ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: While academic excellence is a key strength of our system, it should not be over-emphasised at the expense of other meaningful activities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: First, we must nurture the joy of learning in our children.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This intrinsic motivation will drive them forward to explore and discover their interests and passions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Second, develop in them an entrepreneurial dare so that they will go beyond the classroom, apply their learning to real-world contexts and pursue their passions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Minister Ong will outline our plans in the higher education landscape, to enable learning at every stage of life.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: To support these plans, we must lay strong foundations in school and help our students develop their passions into strengths and to their fullest potential.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Fourth, all of these efforts must be founded upon sound values and character.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We want to nurture individuals who are not only successful, but also committed to their family, to serving the community and to Singapore's future.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Lastly, we must continue to ensure equal access to opportunities for all, regardless of their backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We believe in nurturing the joy of learning so that every child can discover his interests, grow his passions and love what he is doing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: School should not just be about doing well in exams.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It should be an exciting place to acquire knowledge and skills, where learning is fun and with the necessary rigour.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: How are our schools changing our teaching practices and methods to foster joyful learning?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: One, we are encouraging learning through play at the start of every child's education.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: When I visit schools, I am always delighted to see how engaged and energised our primary school students are, when they learn not only in the classroom, but also through lessons in the school gardens, through field trips and outdoor games, and all the different things that I did not have the opportunity to do.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This makes learning come alive and sows the seeds for innovation from primary school onwards.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Beyond the classroom, students can explore further afield through Applied Learning Programmes, such as in robotics, food sciences, media communications, arts and music, and through many, many other avenues.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Through these hands-on activities, sometimes even employing modern technologies, students' learning takes on real-world meaning and relevance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In these ways, students find joy in learning and are intrinsically motivated to learn, not just for examinations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I share Ms Denise Phua's concern about tuition and thank her for her suggestions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Children need to have more unstructured space to play, to grow their imagination, creativity and socio-emotional skills.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: If a child spends too much time on tuition, his holistic development can be impacted.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Excessive tuition can also develop a crutch mentality in our students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This stands in the way of what we want to do to teach them: self-management, self-responsibility and self-reliance in learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I fully understand that parents want to give the best support to help their children do well in their studies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But we need to find a balance, at each age.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As a parent, it is not easy to learn when to step forward to assist our children or when to step back so that they learn independence and self-reliance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Parents like me need to find the balance, and I hope all parents would.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Not yet an e-campus, but we are working towards that.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will also continue to partner self-help groups in the community who have done good work in providing subsidised tutoring to those in need.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But not all students who go for tuition actually need it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: What truly fuels the tuition industry is an unhealthy over-emphasis on academic results that we all need to move away from.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Changes to the Primary School Leaving Examination (PSLE) scoring system, as I have announced last year, are a step in this direction.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Making this paradigm shift towards a more holistic education for our children is not easy and will not be easy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I agree with Mr Lim Biow Chuan that we should not set overly high standards for school examinations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Schools also take care to pitch the language used in their assessments appropriately to avoid penalising students who are weaker in English.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: While schools will do their part, parents, I suggest, would also need to make judicious choices, taking into consideration the child's total needs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I am glad to see a gradual mindset change among parents.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: More are starting to see the value of creating informal, unstructured learning spaces for their children.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I look forward very much to deepening this partnership with parents to cultivate and sustain this joy of learning in our children.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Finding passion is good but we need to do more.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We need to help our students develop an entrepreneurial dare so that they will apply what they learn, act on their passions and pursue them.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Dennis Tan spoke about promoting entrepreneurship in schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our students are exposed to Business and Entrepreneurship through Co-Curricular Activities (CCAs) and Applied Learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: My vision for entrepreneurial dare, however, is broader and goes beyond encouraging entrepreneurship.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is not simply about promoting businesses or startups.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Rather, entrepreneurial dare is an attitude, a mindset of pushing boundaries, of wanting to innovate and finding a breakthrough.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It applies across all domains, not just in business and enterprises, but also in scientific research, engineering and the arts.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: So, it is not about the mechanics of entrepreneurship but a broader foundation to equip our students with that entrepreneurial dare to push boundaries.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Being "entrepreneurial" is about having a spirit of enterprise.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: An enterprising person is able to quickly analyse across complex issues and identify problems and gaps, develop new ideas, seize opportunities and take action.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: To "dare", resilience is key because it is often the fear of failure that holds us back.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: If we are confident of being able to bounce back, more of us will have the resilience to "try, fail, try again" until we succeed.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Adaptability enables us to quickly innovate to seize the opportunities or respond to the challenges that may crop up.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Some employers I have spoken to tell me they want to see more entrepreneurial dare in our students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They say our students are smart, but some are afraid to embrace risks in trying new things or new ways of doing things.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Because it is easy to become hemmed in by our own successes, we must try to help our children venture out of their comfort zones and fail-safe modes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Having entrepreneurial dare is all the more important as we enter uncharted waters ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: To cultivate this entrepreneurial dare, we need to infuse it into our students' education journey and create an environment where trying is encouraged and failing is accepted as a step towards success and as part of our overall learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Outdoor education is one key way to nurture this entrepreneurial dare because it promotes many of the traits required.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In fact, I joined some of them recently.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I joined students from Whitley Secondary School and Tanjong Katong Girls' School when they were at OBS.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Most of them tell me OBS is fun and they also say that it is challenging.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They shared, however, that whether out at sea or in the forest, they are often pushed to the limit, physically and mentally.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In those unfamiliar environments, they had to learn to draw on one another's strengths to overcome challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They have to either try and persevere or remain stuck in uncomfortable situations.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Through these experiences, they tell me they learned to rough it out and emerge together tougher, more confident and resilient.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I am glad to see the MOE-OBS programme developing well.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Parents who got a taste of outdoor activities at MOE's Outdoor Adventure Learning Centres have also given us very positive feedback.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They see how outdoor education can develop resilience and a can-do spirit in their children and are glad that we are investing in this area.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Png Eng Huat asked how we will support and promote sports in schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Students learn how to play a wide range of sports in PE and participate in inter-class games.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Those who are interested can also get into the more vibrant sports scenes that we have engendered in the schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We are also committed to developing sporting strengths.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: MOE's Junior Sports Academy selects primary school students with a high natural ability in sports and grows their talent from a young age.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: If I recall correctly, it is in the region of 400 to 500 of these young primary school students that will join this academy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Applied learning is another way to nurture entrepreneurial dare.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will continue to create more informal, less structured learning spaces, both within and outside of the classroom, for our children to explore and discover the world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Last year, Teck Whye Secondary celebrated its 50th anniversary.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: When I visited, Teck Whyeans proudly showed me a golden orchid.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Because the golden orchid was actually developed by Teck Whyeans − secondary school kids.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They wanted to have this golden orchid to celebrate 50 years of the school's founding.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It took them five years and five different graduating cohorts to breed this golden orchid and, in the process, learn the science of plant genetics.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It took leadership and teamwork across cohorts, with seniors passing this project on to their juniors when they graduated.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It took many rounds of trying and failing.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But when the students eventually succeeded, they were thrilled and immensely proud to present the golden orchid to the school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: When I visited last year, I could see their pride and joy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They showed me what our students can achieve when they can combine academic rigour in our system with the joy of learning, and a dose of entrepreneurial dare.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This simple project of experimentation goes to show the important roles our schools can play in nurturing these qualities.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: MOE is studying how to build on these good practices to further infuse the joy of learning and entrepreneurial dare in our curriculum and teaching practices.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However, there is no silver bullet or any easy one way to foster the joy of learning, entrepreneurial dare and reduce the over-emphasis on academic results.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But as we move in this direction, I hope parents, the wider community and this House will continue to support us in helping our young to discover and pursue their passions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is passion that will sustain our children throughout their education journey.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Fueled by passion, our young can better meet their aspirations and contribute to the future economy as holistic individuals and lifelong learners.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Members are interested to know how we will prepare our students for the growth opportunities that CFE has painted in the region and worldwide.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: To do this, we are committed to developing strengths in every student.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: If they are good at something, we want to help them hone their strengths into deep knowledge and skills.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: By tapping on these strengths and the strong foundations laid in schools, they will be empowered across the multiple post-secondary pathways available.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our strong Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) and bilingual education provide a good base for students to discover their talents and develop their skills.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our young will need deep skills and expertise to harness technology in the future economy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I met some Singaporeans in Silicon Valley during a recent study trip.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They told me that they had always been interested in technology.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: What enabled them to pursue their successful careers in Silicon Valley is the strong core of technical skills and knowledge that they had acquired back home in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our bilingual education also builds strong communication skills that our students can use to connect across cultures, while rooting them in their cultural identity.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For those who build this into a strength, they will be well-positioned to seize opportunities in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), China, India and across the world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
