text: Several Members have asked how we will strengthen our mother tongue languages and cultures and whether we should consider introducing regional languages in our curriculum.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Parliamentary Secretary Low Yen Ling and Parliamentary Secretary Faishal Ibrahim will address some of these issues later.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They will highlight how we are making our mother tongue languages come alive to ignite students' interest.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Because every child is unique and has different aptitudes and learning pace, we need to give our young people different options and diverse paths.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is why we offer some flexibility for secondary school students in the Normal (Academic) and Normal (Technical) courses to take their stronger subjects at a higher academic level.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Today, it is not uncommon for upper secondary students in Normal (Academic) course to take one or two subjects at Express level.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Those in Normal (Technical), likewise, can take subjects at Normal (Academic) level.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In 2014, we extended this flexibility to the lower secondary students in 12 prototype schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Students who have done well in specific subjects at PSLE or in secondary school examinations have the option to take these subjects at a higher level earlier from Secondary 1 and not only from Secondary 3.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Not only does this help them deepen their learning in their areas of strengths, it also helps our students build confidence and opens up new post-secondary possibilities for them.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have since learnt from the prototype experience and are ready to extend this to all secondary schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Dr Intan asked if we should do away with streaming.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I know that there are concerns that streaming can inadvertently discourage some students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But we also know, as Dr Intan has acknowledged, too, that it has served our students well.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Nevertheless, I recognise that we cannot take a one-size-fits-all approach.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We have increased porosity across the various courses.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For the late bloomers, they can transfer to a more demanding course if they are able to cope with the academic requirements of the course.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For students with uneven strengths across the subjects, they can stretch themselves in their areas of strength through subject-based banding.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These are all ways to ensure that our students are not held back but are instead better supported in realising their potential.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I recently met some girls from the Convent of the Holy Infant Jesus (CHIJ) St Theresa's Convent, who shared how they have benefited from Subject-Based Banding.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They told me that taking one or two subjects at a higher level has boosted their confidence in learning and also helped them realise their potential across subjects.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Catrice Gan, who is in the Normal (Academic) course, took English at the Express level when she was in Secondary 1 and enjoyed herself very much in that class, so much so that the experience made her a more confident learner and she improved in her Mathematics and was later offered to study Mathematics at the Express level as well.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: She told me she never imagined this could happen because Mathematics was her weakest subject in PSLE.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Now in Secondary 3, she is looking forward to taking both English and Mathematics at O-Level.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The girls admitted also that adjusting to this faster pace of learning was not always easy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Their teachers and parents provided a lot of support to help them adjust.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Some of them told me they gave it a good shot but, eventually, decided not to continue.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Still, they told me that it was a good learning experience for them and they were glad to be given this opportunity to try.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Lim Biow Chuan and Mr Edwin Tong asked about appeal transfers after the Secondary 1 Posting Exercise.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our transfer process must be fair and transparent.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Secondary 1 Posting Exercise is conducted based on PSLE performance.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Hence, principals will consider appeals only if the student has met the school's cut-off point.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our secondary schools do not only admit students based on cut-off points.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The Direct School Admission (DSA) scheme was set up to allow schools to recognise and admit students based on a more diverse range of talents and achievements, beyond what the PSLE recognises.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Many students take up the DSA because they want to further nurture their talents and strengths through specific programmes in schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: At St Theresa's Convent, I saw how hard the Theresian hockey team fought to win a friendly match.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: A few hockey players I saw told me they joined the school via DSA, because they had fallen in love with hockey at primary school and wanted to further develop their talent through the strong hockey team at St Theresa's Convent.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Like the Theresians who chased their passion, Kirshann Venu Das joined Evergreen Secondary via DSA.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: He wanted to nurture his passion and talent in English through their Communication Programme.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: When Kirshann was in Secondary 2, he won the Silver medal at the National Schools Literature Festival Poetry Slam.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Now a junior college (JC) 2 student, he continues his passion of studying Literature at A-Level and conducts public poetry recitals at school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These examples illustrate the intent of our DSA scheme and how students have benefited by taking ownership of their education choices.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Ang Wei Neng asked for a breakdown of the DSA admission numbers in 2016.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is not surprising, given that IP schools have full discretion in admission, while the majority of our secondary schools can only set aside 5%, 10% or 20% of their Secondary 1 intake for DSA places today, depending on the type of school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our schools, I agree with Mr Ang, have robust distinctive programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For example, the Applied Learning Programmes and the Learning for Life Programmes are designed in consultation with industry partners to offer more authentic learning experiences so that we can do more to help students take advantage of these programmes via DSA in all schools to pursue their interests.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: With this expansion, students can better access schools with suitable programmes via DSA to nurture their strengths, talents and interests.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As Mr Edwin Tong has pointed out, DSA should not be seen as an entry ticket to popular schools, but it is also a mutual commitment between the school and the student, and the child will have to complete the DSA application process before the release of the PSLE results.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will also make changes to the DSA processes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Today, all applicants who apply for a particular DSA category in a school go through the same selection that is open and merit-based.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The selection matches a student's strengths and interests to a school's talent development programmes and ensures that students are able to cope with the academic rigour of the school's programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We will start refining DSA selection from this year to better achieve the objectives of DSA.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As Mr Edwin Tong and some parents have rightly pointed out, students with strong general academic abilities would already be able to qualify for the school with their PSLE results.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: These tests are used by some schools as a standardised assessment of applicants' general reasoning and problem-solving skills.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: While they allow for a comparison of students' abilities, they also inadvertently put undue focus on general academic abilities, rather than identifying specific strengths.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Schools will continue to focus on identifying sporting, artistic or academic talent in specific domains, for instance, the languages, Mathematics or Science.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Schools can conduct their selection via a range of assessment tools, including interviews, trials, auditions and subject tests.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They will also consider the applicant's overall portfolio and achievements.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: A second change we will make is to simplify the DSA application process.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Today, students have to apply to individual schools, each with their own application processes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Schools will also have to put out clear information about the DSA categories and selection criteria on their websites.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This will help students and parents make better informed choices.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I look forward to seeing more primary school students take up these increased opportunities to develop their strengths in a more holistic fashion.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As we improve our education system, we will continue to ensure that it remains open and inclusive, such that every child will have access to a quality education.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This inclusiveness and openness should not be taken for granted.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In many countries, parents are not optimistic that their children will have a good education if they come from the lower socio-economic quartiles.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In the 2015 PISA results, about half of our Singaporean students in the bottom socio-economic quarter were found to be resilient, performing better than what their socio-economic status would otherwise predict.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This is almost twice the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD) average.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We must continue to ensure open access to opportunities for all students, regardless of their backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Minister of State Janil Puthucheary will share more on this later.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Png Eng Huat and Mr Leon Perera asked about MOE's resourcing of schools.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Mr Png said that this is the second year he is asking.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our schools are well-resourced, both in terms of funding and manpower.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Because schools have different student profiles, they run different programmes, catering to different learning needs and learning pace.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In deciding how much to resource, our focus is on the student.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Equitable funding is not about giving every school the same resources, but taking a needs-based approach, varying our resourcing to bring out the best in every child.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This funding goes towards supporting a skills-based curriculum and customised learning environments that can better position the students for subsequent studies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It is also important for me to clarify that the recent mergers were due to falling cohort sizes and not as what the Members have misunderstood them to be.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The mergers were necessary to sustain a critical mass to offer students a good range of educational programmes and quality learning experiences.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We take a needs-based approach in deploying teachers, too.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The size of our teaching force has increased by 20% over the last decade, lowering our pupil-teacher ratios (PTRs) to 16 and 12 at the primary and secondary levels respectively.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Rather than reducing class sizes across the board, schools deploy their additional teachers flexibly to keep class sizes smaller for students who need that extra support.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For instance, in learning support classes for Primary 1 and Primary 2 students who require extra help in English or Mathematics, there are typically only eight to 10 students per class.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: OECD research has shown that teacher quality is, in fact, more critical than class sizes for student outcomes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Hence, we should not focus solely on class sizes but on the overall situation in how we deploy our teachers optimally for the best outcomes for the kids.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I agree with Dr Intan and Dr Lim Wee Kiak that we want to ensure some level of access for students who are interested in secondary schools with affiliation but did not attend the affiliated primary school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Today, 27 secondary schools offer their affiliated primary school students priority in the Secondary 1 posting.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Affiliates qualify for this priority only if they indicate the affiliated secondary school as their first choice.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It helps foster a strong school spirit and preserves the schools' traditions and ethos.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: But notwithstanding these merits, we have to ensure that our schools are open to all students, regardless of their backgrounds or connections.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Since the 2014 Primary 1 Registration Exercise, we have already set aside at least 40 places in every primary school for children without prior connection to the school.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This gives every Singaporean child a better chance to enter the primary school of his choice.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Most affiliated secondary schools today already admit more than 20% of non-affiliates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: However, since this proportion varies up and down, year to year, we are setting aside 20% of places every year in every affiliated secondary school, to strike a balance between recognising affiliation and all the benefits and ensuring open access for all students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: MOE believes in nurturing socially responsible, value-centred Singaporeans who care for their family, community and our Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Our Character and Citizenship Education effort is integrated in the various experiences of school life.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Students are also given opportunities to put their social and emotional competencies into action through their involvement in activities, such as CCAs and Values in Action programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As they reflect on these experiences, our students can better internalise our core values through their experiential learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: (In Mandarin):   Singapore's education system is starting from a position of strength.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It will equip us to respond to the changes and the challenges ahead.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: To better prepare our students for the future, our schools are taking the following broad directions.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: First, we must nurture the joy of learning and an "entrepreneurial dare" in our students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: The joy of learning means that we cultivate an intrinsic interest and passion in students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: This will drive them forward to explore and discover their interests and passions throughout their lifetimes.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Second, with regard to entrepreneurial dare, we will encourage students to try different things and apply their learning to real-world contexts, so that they will learn not to fear failure when facing difficulties and try again and again until final success.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Through this way, students will understand that "failure is the mother of success".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Third, schools must help students lay a strong foundation and help them develop passions into strengths and to their fullest potential.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Values and character continue to remain at the core of all that we do.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: We want to nurture holistic individuals who are not just passionate about learning and work, but also passionate about and committed to Singapore's future and willing to contribute to the nation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Last but not least, we will continue to ensure equal access to opportunities for all, regardless of their background.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Each Singapore child must be able to achieve their full potential.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: (In English): Let me now turn to other issues that Members have raised.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Dr Tan Wu Meng and Miss Cheng Li Hui asked about Singapore International Schools for overseas Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Nevertheless, MOE is committed to supporting children of parents who have ventured abroad.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: MOE helps to get them to stay in touch with the Singapore school system while they are away and also to ease their integration back into the local school system at any time that they return.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: For example, schools allow students to take a Leave of Absence and provide them with teaching and learning materials while they are overseas.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: As more venture overseas, we will see how we can do this better.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: In closing, let me share the story of a group of ITE College West students whom I met recently.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They won the top prize in the national Green Wave Environmental Care competition, beating several other credible teams in the JC-ITE category.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: What impressed me was not just because they had won.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: What really impressed me was how they had discovered their passion and applied their learning in Environmental Sciences.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Determined to repopulate horseshoe crabs in the wild, the team started a school project to improve the hatch rate of the eggs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Through many months of hard work, they developed expertise in this field and discovered new knowledge in the propagation of horseshoe crabs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: It was fascinating to hear from these 18- to 19-year-olds how they harvested the eggs, built their own incubator from recycled materials, complete with an enhanced oxygen hatching tray, to improve the hatch rates.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: When I was talking to them and learning about all these things, I encouraged them to seize this opportunity and make the most out of it.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Maybe, with a little bit of entrepreneurial spirit and some assistance from industry, they can do a startup and extract this and make it a business, make it worthwhile medicinally and do good overall.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Most importantly, when I talked to them as I prepared for this speech, I saw the joy in their eyes and their entrepreneurial dare to push boundaries in their learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: When I reflected on this, I found that their success is not a coincidence.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They had discovered and pursued their passion; they worked hard with the academic rigour that we had instilled in them in school and developed these through project work into a strength.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: They were not deterred by the many failures and challenges and found the tenacity to see through their project.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: I share their story because their journey is exactly what we want all our students to experience: learning with joy, having an entrepreneurial dare and having the strength of character to overcome challenges and setbacks.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Schools) (Mr Ng Chee Meng)
text: Therefore, let us work together, this House and beyond, to nurture our students so that they will become holistic individuals and lifelong learners with deep skills and expertise, ready for the future.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Three-quarters of these students are supported in our mainstream schools and are able to access the same curriculum and opportunities which equip all our children with skills and knowledge for the future economy.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: These students are supported by our Allied Educators and a core group of teachers in each school trained to support children with special needs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong asked about how we train our professionals.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There are key service providers delivering structured training programmes for our school personnel.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOE works with the National Institute of Education (NIE) to provide both pre- and in-service training in special needs for Allied Educators (AEDs) and teachers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) are also involved in providing in-service courses and professional advice.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Perera asked about the challenges faced by schools in engaging bus contractors.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will work with other Government agencies to explore how best to encourage more bus operators to serve SPED students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In the post-secondary space, our Post-Secondary Education Institutions (PSEIs) have SEN Support Offices to support students in securing internships and jobs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our Institutes of Higher Learning (IHLs) also work with SG Enable to provide internship opportunities for students with SEN to build up their professional network and gain practical job-related skills.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: This will support persons with disabilities in continuing training beyond their school years.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The House would be familiar with the School-to-Work transition programme, a collaboration between MOE and SG Enable for work-capable SPED students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The outcomes have been positive and we look forward to more students benefiting from this programme.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I should highlight that such positive outcomes for our students would not have been possible without strong support from our community and industry partners.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Their open hearts and minds have made a big difference to the lives of our SPED students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: I will encourage more partners and employers to step forward and play a part in enabling opportunities for our students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOE tries to be an inclusive employer and is working with SG Enable to explore opportunities to recruit persons with disabilities into more suitable positions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Ms Chia Yong Yong asked about disability awareness, which is an important element of our Character and Citizenship Education curriculum.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: It is useful to set aside time for students to discuss such issues face-to-face with their teachers and peers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: But we do hope to go beyond disability awareness to encouraging our students to appreciate different abilities and to show care towards all.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our schools are also involved in "Values in Action" projects, or in Satellite Partnerships with SPED schools, which allow our students to directly engage and interact with peers of different abilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Gan Thiam Poh and Dr Lim Wee Kiak had asked about our MOE Kindergartens (MKs) which provide quality and affordable preschool education.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The fees are comparable to the Anchor Operators, and eligible children receive assistance from the Early Childhood Development Agency (ECDA), To attract capable educators, MK teachers are remunerated competitively.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Children from MKs have been able to transit well into the primary schools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The experience from running the 15 MKs has been valuable in establishing good practices and in developing teaching and learning resources and for sharing these with the rest of the preschool sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As Minister Ng announced last month, MOE will open another three new MKs in Punggol to serve the high demand there.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We will continue to assess the progress of our pilot MKs and review our plans as part of the Government's overall efforts to strengthen the preschool sector.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh had asked if MOE would implement early detection of dyslexia at the preschool level.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Every year, there are some very young children who need more time to develop fluency in oral language skills, as a result of a number of problems with literacy, including but not limited to, dyslexia.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Such children are actively identified and the focus at the preschool years is then on providing high-quality language and early literacy instruction, without rushing to make a diagnosis for a problem that may be temporary.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The literacy support and interventions can still be carried out and are effective.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: As I had updated the House last year, MOE has expanded the Focused Language Assistance in Reading (FLAiR) programme to support more kindergarten children who have difficulty learning English.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Mr Louis Ng had asked how MOE acts against negligent parents who do not ensure that their child attends school.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: He mentioned the Compulsory Education Act which holds parents responsible for their children's attendance at school.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To date, we have not found it necessary to resort to prosecution.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Beyond formal curriculum hours, Student Care Centres (SCCs), as Dr Lim pointed out, play an important role in providing a conducive after-school environment for our students, including those from disadvantaged backgrounds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Miss Cheng Li Hui had asked about MOE's involvement in NurtureSG and our ongoing efforts to build healthy bodies and healthy minds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: MOE has been working with our schools, community partners and families to build resilience in our students.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: In school, the students themselves, particularly the older students, also play an important role in fostering a caring and supportive environment.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Students in distress may confide first in their friends, who can provide them with a listening ear and critical support in a time of need.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Some of our schools have already taken the lead to strengthen such peer support networks.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We hope to build on this good work and establish the practice across our school system.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Starting from this year, MOE will train a core group of students in each school to establish a caring environment in every class, to identify signs of distress in their peers and offer basic social and emotional support.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We also hope that for this group of "peer supporters", such training and experience will serve as a unique development opportunity to hone their empathetic listening, interpersonal and communication skills.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: They can also help raise awareness of mental well-being amongst their schoolmates and engender a culture of support and resilience in the school where students are willing to seek help.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: There is no single solution to the underlying problems behind mental health issues, which are often complex and, in rare cases, may result in a tragic situation of suicide.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: One of the NurtureSG Task Force's recommendations, therefore, is to set up an interagency workgroup on youth suicide.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Dr Lam Pin Min and I thank Prof Daniel Fung from the Institute of Mental Health (IMH) for agreeing to lead this effort, and I am confident the workgroup's findings will be instructive.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: By the end of this year, all primary and secondary schools, junior colleges and the Millennia Institute will have implemented the "Healthy Meals in Schools Programme" which will allow our students to easily access healthy food options.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh suggested to start school later.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our schools determine their start time and do so based on various factors, including traffic conditions, parents' need to get to work on time after dropping their children off, and the afternoon heat affecting student attention.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: For better health and learning, the key is the amount and quality of sleep our students get.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Lessons on good sleep habits are currently incorporated into our primary school curriculum.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: The importance of sleep and sleep hygiene will also be taught in the secondary school curriculum so that students can exercise self-management.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We also hope to partner parents in instilling good sleep habits and the practice of good sleep hygiene in their children.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We have also been encouraging our students to be active.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Our formal PE curriculum has been increased to at least two hours a week for all schools.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: To provide students with more opportunities for "unstructured play", where they can initiate their own sports and games, our schools will also make available sports equipment and school facilities for our students to use during their break or after school hours.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: Otherwise, these efforts will be unsuccessful and any gains will not be sustained over a child's lifetime.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We need to aim for healthy, active and resilient children who become healthy, active and resilient adults who take on a personal responsibility for their own well-being.

speaker: The Minister of State for Education (Dr Janil Puthucheary)
text: We welcome and thank them for all the efforts and we look forward to a continued and strengthened partnership with many more.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: If implemented effectively, it will sustain Singapore's competitive advantage and help our people ride the waves of significant shifts in jobs and skills throughout their careers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: What has the impact been so far and how can they be scaled up to support more workers?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Of course, Madam, it is far better if our workforce uses SkillsFuture in a proactive manner to prepare, retrain and reskill themselves for industries of the future, rather than wait until their jobs are affected.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, I continue to receive feedback that the SkillsFuture system does not lay out a clear path to follow.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: For a start, people need to know what the future growth clusters are, where future jobs will flourish and what kind of vacancies exist and will emerge.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: How can we better help our citizens position themselves for careers in growth areas and the transition paths, step by step, on what they should do to get there?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There should be clear linkages from training courses to skills and jobs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The range of training courses available in SkillsFuture is wide and the quality is uneven.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There is also the possibility of allowing those who have been trained to add their own rating, so, feedback rating.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: SkillsFuture should also provide tools for career guidance that will help direct people's training efforts towards growth clusters.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Lastly, SkillsFuture is most effective when it is closely linked to specific job requirements.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Companies and trade associations and chambers (TACs) should be encouraged to play a very active role in customising training especially suited to their respective industries.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Government should support TACs on training infrastructure, training design and learning pedagogy that are relevant to their industry to support learning in a modularised fashion, strengthening learning and on the job utilisation.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: What more can be done to encourage both the young and mature Singaporeans to embrace modular training and e-learning?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How can we persuade more Singaporeans to embrace lifelong learning?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How long will it take to change our people's mindset and for them to see the importance of equipping themselves with the relevant skills?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How prepared is the Civil Service sector in recognising qualifications attained through modular courses and e-learning curricula?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Are employers ready to acknowledge new job entrants with skills qualifications obtained through e-learning?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: How do we change both employers' and employees' mindset to accept such training as a way of life for Singaporeans to keep pace with the changing skills needs of the economy and achieve skills mastery?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: To see a significant change in the mindset of employers, I urge the Civil Service and the Government-linked companies to initiate and lead by example.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: In the healthcare sector, too, there should be pervasive modular training and e-learning modules for support staff to strive to upgrade themselves for career progressions.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: However, as more take on skills-based programmes, the professional regulatory bodies must stand prepared to review the current programmes and provide greater accessibility to modular training and e-learning.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: To prevent "a spiraling paper chase" and producing a workforce which excels in exams but are ill-equipped to take on jobs of the future, there is a need for our society to move away from exam-based assessment and provide greater emphasis on practical training.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: We should also allow funding and subsidies to be extended to standard programmes of modular and e-learning curricula.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Workers in employment who pursue programmes of such nature must be given equal opportunity for recognition, promotion and career progression.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: I trust the Government to also change the mindset of human resource professionals to be inclusive in their recruitment of job applicants with skills-based qualifications obtained through e-learning and short courses.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Now, I wish to also speak on women in male-dominated sectors.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Information and communications technology (ICT) is a fast-growing sector for Singapore.

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Does the Ministry have data to show a comparison on the usage of SkillsFuture Credits across gender?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: If so, is there any significant difference between the genders for ICT and STEM programmes?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Does the Government also curate the courses to ensure that they are up to date and relevant, given the rapidly changing nature of technology?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Have there been efforts to encourage women mid-career switchers who go for conversion programmes to consider STEM-related training?

speaker: Ms K Thanaletchimi (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Ministry consider allocating STEM scholarships for female students?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It will be inevitable that practical outcomes would be expected of SkillsFuture and sought after in view of dire warnings of machines replacing people and the requirement for a high level of skills to succeed in the workplace of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The concern I have then and as I do now is that Singaporeans do not see a qualification strategy as being synonymous with the genuine skills upgrading strategy.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To that end, the review mechanism to understand the outcomes of SkillsFuture is a necessity.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As the Government has shared, SkillsFuture is more than just a movement targeted at specific age groups but across age groups and society and, therefore, it is also about the larger cultural shift towards lifelong learning.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Can the Ministry provide more details about this number in terms of the types of courses taken up by Singaporeans and the age group breakdown of Singaporeans who have used their SkillsFuture Credits?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: While I accept it would be more important for Singaporeans to utilise their credits carefully and thoughtfully, can the Minister comment on his assessment of the utilisation rates so far?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In reply to my Parliamentary Question, the Minister also replied that it dedicates far more funds to subsidising course fees at the supply end to make them affordable, not just SkillsFuture credits, so that there are avenues for workers to reskill or upgrade.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In addition, does the Ministry dovetail newly subsidised courses with the various Industry Transformation Roadmaps (ITMs) under the broad strategic direction offered by CFE?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If so, is the Ministry considering stepping up public communication to advise Singaporeans of the options available to take up courses for new careers and for those who change careers midway through their working life?

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: It is clear they were aware of the need to retrain and upgrade themselves.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: What is worrying is that the increase was driven by professionals, managers, executives and technicians (PMETs).

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: However, it is even more urgent for the lower-skilled workers to upskill and retrain.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: I am very concerned about those whose jobs will likely be eliminated due to technological advances, such as drivers, receptionists, telemarketers and waiters.

speaker: Miss Cheng Li Hui (Tampines)
text: How does the Ministry reach out to these groups of Singaporeans?

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: An oft-cited reason given by young women for putting off having children is that they are concerned that parenthood may permanently derail their careers.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Women tend to find it more difficult to re-enter the workforce after having children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Now, with the constant stress to upgrade one's skills so as to remain competitive and stay relevant, more pressure is placed upon women who question if they can afford to take time off and still be able to keep up with their peers when they return.

speaker: Assoc Prof Daniel Goh Pei Siong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This award will encourage mothers to take up training that may help them remain relevant to their industries, keep their skills sharp and make re-entry into the workforce a little less challenging.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: While the Government may point to the existence of the Central Provident Fund (CPF) Education Scheme as a similar initiative, there are several limitations of the scheme such that it does not adequately address the needs of working adults who may wish to further their education or to take up training courses.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: One such limitation is the type of courses that it applies to.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: On top of this, the use of CPF to fund education and training will also have an impact on the retirement adequacy of the individual and their family members, if they are still eligible to borrow from the CPF savings of their parents or spouse.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: In the implementation of the SkillsFuture Education Loan, some aspects can be borrowed from the CPF Education Scheme, such as pegging of interest rates to CPF Ordinary Account interest rates, which are less onerous than rates offered by banks, and stipulating that repayment will commence a year after graduation.

speaker: Mr Low Thia Khiang (Aljunied)
text: The loan scheme will give individuals greater peace of mind over repayment which may, in turn, encourage more people to pursue retraining or higher education.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: As an open economy, Singapore will inevitably be affected.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: There are concerns among Singaporeans that these uncertainties will cause disruptions to our livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Parents will also be concerned about how their children can be prepared for future jobs.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: To prepare ourselves for the future, CFE has recommended that we deepen and diversify our international connections and acquire and utilise deep skills.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our education system must provide the opportunities for our students to be exposed to the region.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Learning and development cannot be limited to the classroom.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Our students must also get out of the classroom and get real work experience.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Many of us will agree that some life skills, such as working with different people, can only be honed through experience and practice, and not just acquired based on theory.

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: How does the Ministry prepare students for future jobs, particularly with regard to applied learning that allows them to learn on the job?

speaker: Mr Zainal Sapari (Pasir Ris-Punggol)
text: Additionally, do our students have the opportunity to take part in overseas programmes so that they can learn more about the cultures and business environments in neighbouring countries?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: I heard inspiring personal stories about the strength of this system from chief executive officers (CEOs) of Swiss multinational companies to SME owners who came up through the ranks of vocational apprenticeship.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: One striking example was a young 16-year-old engineer employed in robotics design in a leading Swiss company whilst pursuing his engineering studies.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: I am encouraged by the emergence of work-study degree programmes in Singapore, with different models being piloted by our local universities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: How can our universities accelerate their efforts and develop the necessary infrastructure, which must include career offices and linkages to industry to expand and support work-study programmes?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Work-study degree programmes can only be successful with the active involvement of employers and their management teams.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Apart from the lack of know-how, such willingness to nurture talent is not yet, unfortunately, ingrained in the corporate culture of most local companies.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Managers tend not to see it as their responsibility or understand how it benefits everyone in the ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Perhaps, the inflexion point will come with the first batches of managers who are themselves beneficiaries of the work-study programmes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Could the Government, Singapore's largest employer, set a shining example in its own ranks?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: During my Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS), many young residents come to appeal for admission into ITE courses.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The Earn and Learn programme is an excellent apprenticeship scheme, where ITE graduates are able to work at participating companies to earn a decent income while learning as an apprentice.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: After a few years of working, many ITE graduates typically want to upgrade to a diploma.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is appropriate, given that they have acquired deeper skills in their respective vocations.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mdm Chairman, a good vocational education is an important foundation of Singapore's economic development.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Over the past 50 years or so, our educational system has undergone perpetual adjustments in line with changes.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Now, the Singapore economy is experiencing a major transformation once again.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This leads us to ponder over how the educational organisations could support industry transformation.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Last year, when the Singapore Chinese Chamber of Commerce and Industry (SCCCI) organised the Trade Association Congress, we invited a business leader from a German Chamber of Commerce as one of our guest speakers.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This friend briefed us on the operational model and experiences of German trade associations.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: In the area of vocational education, the German industry associations play a powerful role.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Industry associations are also invested with much authority.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: They provide practical vocational training, with a key focus on grooming specialised technical personnel.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Certificates issued by industry associations are recognised by society and become important references in the recruitment of workers.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: Like Singapore, SMEs make up 99% of all business entities in Germany.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, the government also provides requisite funding to industry associations.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: People always rave about that German workers are well-trained and, in this regard, the industry associations have contributed a great deal.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: With compulsory membership in industry associations, both large enterprises and SMEs are thrust together in the same boat.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: With sound financial foundations and deep insights into the industry, trade associations would be able to tackle the pains of economic restructuring in a timely manner and with greater accuracy.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This is also one of the reasons why the German manufacturing industry can remain strong all this time.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: I hope the Government could authorise trade associations to conduct even more vocational skills training courses.

speaker: Mr Thomas Chua Kee Seng (Nominated Member)
text: This would constitute another milestone, bringing the national education system more in step with a transforming era.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: I have met residents whose families spent a small fortune on a degree from a private institution.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: In some cases, the parents withdrew CPF savings, retirement savings to support their children on the course.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: It is important to know whether they got value for money.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: How detailed is MOE's tracking of educational outcomes for private degrees as well as skills upgrading?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: Does MOE look at skills upgrading outcomes and whether the skills learnt are actually being used at work later on?

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: We must distinguish between providers who are only selling hope rather than skills and opportunities.

speaker: Dr Tan Wu Meng (Jurong)
text: This will help us better support students, parents and responsible constructive education providers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: However, in the push to improve our ranking results, have we lost sight of more important goals?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: One of the main reasons why NUS and NTU have improved their rankings was their push for their professors to produce academic papers that can be cited by acclaimed international academic journals.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Is this done at the expense of having the professors conduct research on local issues, which are less glamorous and would less likely be published in the international journals?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Has the concentration on showy research compromised the quality of teaching?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: The local universities are heavily funded by the Government.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: I know that the grant focuses on big themes with a public purpose, such as social integration and resilience, building identities, developing new models of training and education and spurring growth, productivity and innovation.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: While these initiatives are significant, I would also like to know whether some of these grants would be available for initiatives that encourage or promote an interest in the Humanities per se and not necessarily the Social Sciences as such and, therefore, lacking in immediate societal outcomes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: This might include historical research on the South China Sea, urban and rural communities in Southeast Asia, Asian literature and languages which encompass a broadening of the knowledge base of Singaporean researchers and institutions, thereby producing independent outcomes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: Such work may not have direct relevance now, but they would be of consequence in view of our geopolitical realities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: What such funding would also do is to generate significant interest among young Singaporeans who seek to pursue postgraduate qualifications to teach and carry out research in our local universities.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: A community of Singaporean Social Science and Humanities scholars with specific expertise would, in time, also raise the quality of the standard of our research, staff and faculty in Singapore and promote a drive towards excellence.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: There should be no reason why the world's pre-eminent historians, sociologists and other humanities specialists of the region should be teaching in a university or institution which is not based in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh
text: We should aim to count as many Singaporeans as we can among such a group of scholars.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Chairman, current admissions to our IHLs are still primarily based on academic results.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is a transparent and objective system but too much stress is placed on our students and parents for these high-stake examinations.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Aptitude-based admissions allow for a more holistic assessment of students and reduce the over-emphasis on academic results.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It takes into consideration the level of passion and interest the students have for their choice of courses.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I am pleased to note the gradual expansion of the aptitude-based admissions to PSEIs, as announced by Minister Ong Ye Kung last year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: He has come to see me two years in a row because, each year, NUS had rejected his application to read Pharmacy at NUS.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: He was told that his grades were not as good as those of the other applicants.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I understand that MOE has started to have Aptitude-based Admissions in PSEIs.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: I have heard some happy stories after the new scheme has started.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: This would be of great help to adult Singaporeans who may not have done well in school but have done very well in their jobs and want a second chance at obtaining an academic qualification.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: More and more young people are interested in creative arts tertiary education, which augurs well for our endeavour to transform Singapore into a Distinctive Global City for the Arts.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Creative arts education fosters creativity and innovation, both necessary for a future-ready Singapore.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I am heartened to note that the Government is looking at how to further develop creative arts tertiary education, both in terms of expanding the scope and depth.

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Would the Ministry provide an update on its plans to enhance the quality of creative arts tertiary education?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How have the enrolments been for the various disciplines and levels at our institutions?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition, what measures does the Ministry have to align our creative arts graduates' skills with industry demands?

speaker: Mr Gan Thiam Poh (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How does the Ministry help them prepare for their future careers and what kind of projects has the Government initiated or attracted to Singapore to help provide them with good career prospects?

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: There is also no denying that the arts stimulate creativity, reimagination and out-of-the box innovation.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: These traits are crucial to Singapore as we look towards the future economy which will be challenging.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We need to nurture the appreciation of arts and culture from a young age.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: We see an improvement in literacy when young people take part in drama and library activities and better performance in Mathematics and Languages when they take part in structured music activities.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: The relationship has been studied and it is undeniable.

speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
text: Hence, what steps are being considered to foster the appreciation of arts and culture amongst our students at an early age?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: (In Mandarin):   The tuition fees charged by PSEIs, especially university tuition fees, have increased significantly over the last 10 years.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: While we understand the need to increase tuition fees to better reflect the value of tertiary industry, we have to be mindful that students from the underprivileged families may be unfairly disadvantaged.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: Income of low-income families usually rises slower than that of upper middle-income families, and a university education is the best way for students from low-income families to go up the ladder.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: This does not just apply to students from low-income families but those who are in the sandwich group or who marginally miss out on MOE's financial assistance scheme because of the qualifying criteria.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng
text: To help such students from the sandwich group, I have to raise funds every year to provide them with bursaries.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will try to answer as many of them as possible in my speech.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I think is a story that many Members already know.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is the story of Ms Kirsten Tan, one of Singapore's most renowned film makers.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I want to tell it again even though Members might be familiar, because there are so many aspects of her story that are so relevant to our education system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Kirsten had always wanted to make films, but her parents, in her own words, these are not my words but her parents', "die die wanted her to go to university".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: So, she went to study literature in NUS but never gave up on film.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: At NUS, she set up her own production house and also set up her own studio.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She made two films and, in her words again, the films were so bad even she did not know what they were all about.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: After NUS, she went to Ngee Ann Polytechnic to do an Advanced Diploma in Film Production.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This time, she made two more films which won awards at the Singapore International Film Festival.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Later, one of her films, as you would know, called "Pop Aye", won a Special Jury Prize at the Sundance film festival.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It was a moment of great pride and joy for her, her family, as well as for Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, she gets gigs from all over the world, mostly work from New York.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I have set up a meeting with her sometime later this year.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And her parents have come round to supporting her in her film-making career.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I tell this story because of the contradictions that she has to deal with in this new world.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Her story is one of pragmatism versus her passion; of parents' expectations versus what she herself so wanted to do; of lifelong upgrading and yet not conforming to the social notion that after a Degree, there must be a Masters or a PhD.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: She went to do an Advanced Diploma in an area she wants to be good at, of venturing beyond Singapore and yet remaining Singaporean at heart.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It is a story of what education should and can do for all of us, across every field.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We have an effective and internationally well-regarded education system.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But sometimes, a great strength can also be a weakness.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: It gives rise to a temptation that maybe we just tinker around the edges when, actually, more fundamental changes may be needed.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I believe that we are at the threshold of major changes in our society and economy.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And the two need not be at odds with one another.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Ms Thanaletchmi made this point very well, although she spoke quite fast.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we must recognise that the learning needs and habits of adult learners are vastly different from those of students.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: For adult learners, it has to be short, concise, modular, convenient and accessible and to the point.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Today, information we can google, skills we cannot.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And whether you are performing a surgery, coding a complex computer programme, cooking something for your clients and for your customers, repairing a car, negotiating effectively or working in a team of people of different cultures, all these are skills.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We are used to the idea of "learning for doing".

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We study for a few years, then we step out into the workforce and we work as a professional, technician or whatever.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But technical and cognitive abilities can also be gained through actual experience.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This method has underlined centuries of European apprenticeship, as Ms Foo Mee Har and Mr Thomas Chua have mentioned.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And it is more important and more relevant than ever today.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Fifth, help Singaporeans adapt to a data-rich and digital working environment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Not everyone needs to learn how to code or become an IT expert.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But we must all be comfortable and competent working in a digitally-enabled working environment.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In other words, we must be data-enabled as a workforce.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These shifts are the building blocks of transformation.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To implement them, we will do three things − build, configure and scale.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: These represent the three overlapping phases of our work.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: First, we need to build, meaning to lay the critical foundations of organisations, structure and funding.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Fortunately, we have been at it for over a decade.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In the early 2000s, the Government set up the Lifelong Learning Endowment Fund.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We set up a dedicated agency to promote lifelong learning, that is, the Singapore Workforce Development Agency (WDA).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: WDA, in turn, set up the Workforce Skills Qualification (WSQ) framework and also set up over 40 training centres to deliver adult training.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Last year, WDA was restructured into two Statutory Boards.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: One of them, SSG, is now part of MOE.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: With that change, education and learning from young to old, for your whole lifetime, comes under one Ministry.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Under this structure, PSEIs under MOE, namely, ITEs, polytechnics and universities, are all given a mandate to promote and drive lifelong learning.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: In 2014, the Singapore Institute of Technology (SIT) became our fifth autonomous university (AU) and the first to pioneer an applied degree pathway.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We will also further develop tertiary education opportunities in the arts.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Mr Edwin Tong and Mr Gan Thiam Poh have asked about this.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: We can do more to develop the capabilities of our two publicly-funded arts institutions, the Nanyang Academy of Fine Arts (NAFA) and LASALLE College of the Arts (LASALLE).

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I will ask Parliamentary Secretary Faishal Ibrahim to talk more about this later in his speech.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Another important aspect of build is to fund lifelong learning, to make it affordable and accessible to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: I have been trying to explain that for a long time.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But I think it is worthwhile spending a bit of time again explaining the concept and how it all works.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Supply-side funding means we fund the training provider so that the course fee charged is lowered to a small fraction of the original cost.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This is not different from the way we fund education or healthcare, which is through schools and hospitals.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The advantage of supply-side funding is that we have better control in funding the courses which are relevant to the industries that represent the growth areas and, very importantly, as pointed out by Mr Singh, aligned to our ITMs.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The downside is that it is not very visible to the public.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The other way is demand-side funding, where funding goes directly to the learner and to the individual.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Examples are bursaries, SkillsFuture Study Awards and, of course, SkillsFuture Credit.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: What is good about demand-side funding is that it is very visible and people do get excited.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: When SkillsFuture Credit was first implemented, people were talking about what they should learn next.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: But the first downside is that if it is done across the board, like SkillsFuture Credit, it can be expensive, that is why we limit it to $500 per Singaporean.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: The second downside is that we have little control on how people will spend the grant.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: This, therefore, gives rise to the question that Ms Foo Mee Har asked: with so many courses, where do I go, and what is it that can help me link up my training with my employability?

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: And what people spend on may not be entirely aligned with our industry and growth strategies.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: To illustrate how it all works, take a training programme that costs $1,000.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
text: Supply-side funding is $900, so the course fee gets lowered to $100.

speaker: The Minister for Education (Higher Education and Skills) (Mr Ong Ye Kung)
